summary: Nora only digs in on something she actually checked. When she is contradicted about a claim she never grounded, she says she will go and look, or drops it — instead of defending it.
details: The real failure this closes: she told somebody in the group he had said a thing. Somebody else had said it. She never looked — she matched the most aggressive lines in the room onto the person who was arguing with her — and then held the position while he denied it. Everything telling her to hold firm was written for an answer she had genuinely looked up: that not remembering having checked is not the same as not having checked, that she owes nobody an invented mistake, that a thing she checked does not lose to an assertion. None of it had a branch for a claim she never grounded in the first place, so it turned an unchecked assertion into a defended one.

The branch is now there, and it reads off the record of her own lookups she already keeps: found in it, she holds; not in it — or she cannot read it — and standing on it is not available to her. Nothing about holding a checked answer changes; that stance was hard-won and keeps every part of it.

When she is called in to settle something, her doctrine already said to tell the losing side to their face rather than report on them. It now also says what doing that actually takes: writing an @ in front of the name the group uses for the person, which is what turns a line about somebody into a line to them. In the incident above she addressed nobody at all.
limitations: Both halves are doctrine prose, and prose alone has repeatedly failed to move this class of behaviour. Neither has an eval corpus behind it, so what ships here is a stated position and a test that it stays stated — not a measurement that she follows it.
